..The upper pattern this morning is defined by a
strong upper-low centered across southeast California and 
Hurricane Polo (a category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained 
winds of 110 mph near 25.9N/112.2W or over the southern Baja 
Peninsula, moving NE at 11 kts). Polo is forecast to rapidly 
weaken as it accelerates toward the NE today, moving south of 
Hermosillo Mexico as a category 1 hurricane by 29/12Z this 
morning, then south of the New Mexico Bootheel in NW Chihuahua
MX as a remnant low by 30/00Z this afternoon. 

The latest satellite and radar imagery indicated a band of showers
with a few embedded thunderstorms that extend from Organ Pipe to
Casa Grande to Globe early this morning which coincide with a 
deformation/lift axis aloft (between 500-300 mb). Elsewhere, 
there are a batch of scattered showers and thunderstorms developing
across west-central and southwest Arizona that are associated 
with the generalized lift out ahead of the core of the upper-
low in SE CA. The latest GOES precipitable water imagery 
indicated deep tropical moisture across Southeast Arizona with 
PWATs 1.50-1.75 inches extending through central Pima county 
into Pinal county and PWATs 1.25-1.50 inches elsewhere across 
Southeast Arizona. 

Showers and thunderstorms start becoming widespread across Southeast
Arizona around daybreak this morning as the upper-low moves southeast,
elongates/amplifies along western Arizona and becomes more neutrally
oriented. This will shift that deformation band/axis east, 
setting up along a line from the southern Baboquivari Mountains
to Three Points to the Catalina Mountains to Bylas. 

This is where things get interesting. With that deep plume of 
tropical moisture to the SW of Tucson and strengthening 
pressure gradients in the low-to-mid levels as the trough re-
orients, we begin to see an area of strong moisture flux 
convergence develop in the lower-levels (850-700mb). This 
moisture convergence will be broad over the majority of 
Southeast Arizona, but will especially enhance convection and 
increase the potential for additional storms to develop and move
over the same area in that aforementioned area of 
deformation/lift aloft. So, initially we will see light to 
moderate rainfall in this band early this morning becoming more 
moderate intensity after daybreak. Then during the mid-morning,
rainfall intensity will pick up again and become moderate to 
heavy. This will then persist into the early afternoon with the 
surface front itself eventually swinging from west to east 
across Southeast Arizona impacting this area again. 

This line is particularly concerning today. This is supported 
by the 29/00Z HREF 3-hr QPF PMM neighborhood probabilities in 
this area, with probabilities between 70-90% for 1.00+ inch at 
the 15Z, 18Z and 21Z time intervals. In addition, there is a 
10% probability for 3.00+ inches at both the 15Z and 18Z time 
frames. That is a major bullseye for the HREF, and it has been 
showing a line like this develop for several model-runs which 
increases my confidence in something big happening. It can be 
5-15 miles east or west of this line, but as it is currently 
aligned, this would specifically impact the Altar/Black/Brawley 
Washes that are the more flood-prone locations to the SW and W 
of Tucson. If it is farther east, this will significantly impact
the NW half of the Tucson Metro Area and the Catalina Mountains
(i.e CDO, Sabino Creek, Tanque Verde Creek). At this time, the 
official forecast is for 1.50-2.50 inches along and near this 
line with up to 3.00-3.50 inches in the higher terrain. Given 
these amounts over a widespread area, flash flooding is a major 
concern. 

Elsewhere, heavy rainfall will impact the entire forecast area
as widespread showers and thunderstorms occur with the general
deformation aloft associated with the approaching trough as well
as the surface frontal band that swings thru the area from west
to east this afternoon. Rainfall runoff will result in running 
water in normally dry washes and roadway dips with significant 
ponding of water likely in low-lying areas and other flood-prone
locations. Isolated to scattered locations may experience flash
flooding with this event. Longer-term heavy flows will also be 
possible tonight into Wednesday within the main-stem drainages 
due to widespread heavy rainfall. There is a Flash Flood Watch 
in effect through 11 PM MST this evening.

Not to be lost in the mix, severe storms will be possible this 
afternoon but should be considered a secondary threat compared 
to the risk of flash flooding. As the upper-level low tracks 
across the area, decent forcing, marginal CAPE and abundant 
shear will be present. Therefore, expect strong to perhaps 
isolated severe storms with brief low-top supercells possible.
